planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plugs in spring into sandy, well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; pineland twinflower spreads gently by rhizomes to form a low, informal groundcover in pine flatwoods and open sandy sites.

directions: Plant in sandy, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; pineland twinflower is a low, spreading Gulf Coast and Florida native groundcover with small, oblong leaves and delicate, pale lavender-blue, funnel-shaped flowers produced in loose pairs nearly continuously through the warm months. It is the primary larval host plant for the common buckeye butterfly in much of its range, so expect and welcome some caterpillar feeding as part of supporting a full butterfly life cycle rather than a purely ornamental planting. Spreading gently by rhizomes, it knits together into a soft, low groundcover under open pines and in sunny to lightly shaded sandy beds, tolerating both drought and the periodic light fire regimes of its native flatwoods habitat. Cut back by about half in late winter to refresh the planting before the new season's growth and bloom begin.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; violet wild petunia is a well-behaved native alternative to the aggressively self-seeding Mexican petunia (Ruellia simplex) sold widely in nurseries.

directions: Direct sow into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; violet wild petunia is a true Texas and Gulf South native wildflower with narrow, hairy leaves and funnel-shaped, violet-purple flowers that open in the morning and typically drop by afternoon, refreshing with new blooms daily over a long spring-through-fall season. It serves as a larval host for the common buckeye butterfly and is visited regularly by native bees, offering solid wildlife value without the aggressive rhizomatous spread of the widely sold, non-native Mexican petunia often confused with it. Plants form a modest, well-mannered clump rather than running aggressively, making them safe to place in mixed beds without fear of them taking over neighboring plants. Cut back hard after the first hard freeze in colder parts of its range, mulching the crown, since it dies back to the roots and resprouts in spring.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions after last frost into average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; creeping sage spreads by trailing stems that root as they go, forming a low mat rather than an upright clump.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; creeping sage is a low, trailing Gulf Coast and Caribbean native salvia with small, scalloped leaves and small, pale lavender-blue flowers produced over a long warm-season bloom, spreading by stems that root wherever they touch soil to form a loose, informal groundcover mat. Unlike the many upright shrubby salvias grown for cut flowers or hummingbird gardens, it is valued mainly as a soft-textured, low-maintenance filler for the front of a bed, between stepping stones, or cascading over a low wall. It dies back with hard freezes but generally returns from surviving stem sections and roots where winters stay above the coldest end of its range, making a protective mulch layer worthwhile at the northern edge of zone 8. Trim back after flowering flushes to keep the mat dense and encourage repeat bloom.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into lean, well-drained, dry, rocky or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; Drummond's false pennyroyal is a small, short-lived native mint of dry Texas and Southwest prairies and rocky slopes.

directions: Direct sow into lean, sharply drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; Drummond's false pennyroyal is a small, wiry, intensely aromatic native mint relative found on dry limestone slopes and prairies from Texas through the Southwest, releasing a strong, minty-camphor scent when the foliage is brushed or crushed. Tiny, tubular, pale lavender to pink flowers appear in the leaf axils from spring through fall, adding subtle color to a dry rock garden or xeriscape planting rather than serving as a showy bedding flower. Historically used in folk medicine as a tea and traditional remedy, it is grown today mostly for its fragrance, drought tolerance, and value as a low, textural filler among rocks and gravel mulch. It is short-lived but self-sows readily in loose, undisturbed soil, so allow some plants to set seed each year to maintain a self-renewing population.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in fall to take advantage of winter rains, into well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; coyote mint is a California chaparral and woodland-edge native with a strong minty-oregano fragrance.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; coyote mint is a low, mounding California native with soft, gray-green, strongly aromatic foliage carrying a fragrance somewhere between mint and oregano, released readily when the leaves are brushed. Dense, rounded clusters of pale lavender-pink flowers cover the plant from summer into fall, drawing large numbers of native bees and butterflies, including numerous specialist pollinators adapted to the mint family. It is well suited to dry, sunny slopes, rock gardens, and low-water borders once established, needing little more than good drainage and occasional deep watering during the longest dry spells. Shear lightly after the main flowering flush to keep growth compact and encourage a second, lighter bloom later in the season.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in fall into well-drained, humus-rich, average soil in partial shade; hummingbird mint spreads gently by trailing stems to form a loose groundcover mat under open woodland canopy.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade beneath open woodland canopy; hummingbird mint is a trailing California native groundcover with small, aromatic leaves and, unusually for the genus, brilliant scarlet-red tubular flowers rather than the lavender or pink typical of most monardellas, an adaptation that draws hummingbirds rather than the bees favored by its purple-flowered relatives. Low, spreading stems root as they trail across the ground, gradually knitting together into a loose mat useful for softening the edges of shaded rock outcrops, woodland paths, or dry streambeds. It needs more consistent moisture and shade than most of its sun-loving, drought-tolerant monardella relatives, reflecting its native habitat in the dappled light of oak woodland and chaparral margins. Water occasionally through the dry season to keep foliage from crisping, and trim lightly after bloom to keep the mat tidy.
